key_gap: Both sides identified the same root cause (a 14:00 reconciliation job, queue-delayed to 14:02, holding row locks on the orders table; the ~3% of checkout requests touching those rows hit the 30 s timeout; provider folklore falsified by the absence of outbound calls in timed-out traces) and proposed the same fix. The human won on experiment-design discipline: it paired every hypothesis with its specific falsifying observation, ranked tests by information-per-unit-cost (a 2-minute cron+lock-wait snapshot before any 20-minute sampling), used the 14:02-vs-14:00 timing offset as a first-class falsifier of the folklore window, ran the decisive same-window control split (orders-touching 3% vs 0%), and closed with an explicit update ledger — which observation killed which hypothesis. The AI ran the same probes but ordered them by availability rather than discrimination power, added a redundant verification pass, and only flagged the timing tell in passing at REVIEW instead of using it as evidence in WHY.
learning_signal: Strong inference, not just hypothesis testing: before running anything, every hypothesis must carry the specific observation that would falsify it, and experiments must be ranked by information value per unit cost — the cheapest test that discriminates between the currently-live hypotheses wins (a 2-minute snapshot can beat a 20-minute profile when it splits the hypothesis space). The canonical discriminating design is a control split: partition the affected population by the suspect feature within the same window and compare. Folklore and vendor claims are hypotheses with priors, not facts — timing inconsistencies (onset 14:02 vs claimed 14:00) are evidence, and falsified hypotheses must be retired with a stated reason. Closing the loop requires an explicit update ledger (observation → hypothesis killed → remaining set) before acting on the survivor.
suggested_improvement: In WHY, require a falsification table: each hypothesis paired with its falsifying observation and probe cost. In HOW, rank candidate experiments by (information value / cost) and execute the cheapest discriminator first; when the suspect feature partitions the population, mandate the same-window control split. Add a 'timing/consistency check' micro-step: compare claimed schedules (vendor windows, cron times) against observed onset and treat any mismatch as evidence against the claim. In REVIEW, add an 'update ledger' line — which observation overturned which hypothesis — so the revision is auditable and the decision packet states why the survivor survived.

key_gap: The pure style failed on both of its registered weaknesses simultaneously. Tempo: it insisted on a 15–20-minute discriminating APM experiment before any action under a ~$40k/hr burn (≈$13k per test), even declaring NEEDS_EVIDENCE and requesting another 20 minutes while the system degraded. Hypothesis-space blindness: the hypothesis set was built from the dashboard (deploy regression, DB contention, traffic, in-app fault) and excluded the outbound layer and non-deploy changes, so all probes returned clean nulls — which the style misread as 'hypotheses eliminated, keep observing' instead of 'the frame excludes the cause.' The AI won with two gates: a META tempo branch (probes ≤ 3 min, ≤ 2 probes before acting, mitigation in parallel with evidence preservation) and a WHY null-pattern trigger (three clean in-service nulls → widen the frame → 1-minute outbound queue-depth probe + 'what changed outside the service in 2 h' → the geo-fence batch job → kill it → P99 recovered in ~5 min, verified by queue drain + recovery curve).
learning_signal: Null results across the entire modeled space are evidence about the frame, not about the world: after two or more clean nulls, the correct inference is 'the hypothesis space is too narrow', not 'the system is healthy' — widen it to outbound dependencies, queue/backlog metrics, and non-deploy changes before concluding anything. Separately, method tempo must track decision tempo: when the burn rate exceeds the experiment cost, action on the most probable cause (reversible, evidence-preserving) plus a cheap parallel probe beats waiting for confirmation; rigor that demands a fully confirmed cause before acting is a liability, and post-action verification (recovery curve, queue drain) is a legitimate experiment. 'We must not contaminate the measurement' can become an excuse for inaction.
suggested_improvement: In META, add a tempo branch keyed on stakes and time-sensitivity: if stakes ≥ HIGH and the environment is live-degrading, set a hard experiment budget (e.g., each probe ≤ 3 min, ≤ 2 probes before acting) and route to 'act now on best probable cause with reversible, evidence-preserving mitigation; verify post-action.' In WHY, add a null-pattern trigger: on the second consecutive clean probe across the modeled space, execute a frame-widening checklist — (a) what changed outside the service in the last T hours (job-runner audit log, non-deploy changes), (b) queue/backlog and outbound-dependency metrics, (c) 'what observable exists that our current probes cannot see?' — and record the widened space before running further tests.
